title: The Lit Windows of Amberlight
logline: When Amberlight House lights its windows after six years dark, the parish decides its new master is hiding a madwoman, when he is only hiding his own kindness.
promise: A shuttered house, a family that will not explain itself, and a perfectly ordinary reason for all of it, arrived at only after the whole parish has guessed wrong.

cast.name: Miss Phoebe Langton
cast.station: dressmaker who takes work through the draper's counter; no fortune beyond her needle
cast.want: to be dealt with as a tradeswoman of skill and honesty, not managed or pitied by her betters
cast.appearance: Twenty-five, small and quick-handed, fair hair pinned under a plain cap, a measuring tape looped always at her wrist.
cast.dress: A grey stuff gown with a clean linen apron, sleeves turned back for work.
cast.voice_note: brisk and plain-spoken, sharpest when she feels looked down on

cast.name: Mr Edward Harker
cast.station: trustee for his young ward's bequest from the late Sir Edward Marchmont's estate; holds the main block of Amberlight House by the Marchmont family's leave; a modest independence of his own
cast.want: to shield his ward from parish talk about her broken engagement without ever having to explain the cruelty behind it
cast.appearance: Thirty-six, tall and spare, close-cropped dark hair going grey at the temple, a guarded face that rarely settles into ease.
cast.dress: A plain dark coat of good cloth, no ornament, boots still carrying the mud of the road.
cast.voice_note: clipped and formal, drops the guard only when his ward is frightened

cast.name: Miss Augusta Fairfax
cast.station: orphaned ward, heiress to a bequest left her by the late Sir Edward Marchmont; no connection to the Marchmont name
cast.want: to be left to grieve quietly until she can face the parish without shame
cast.appearance: Nineteen, slight and fair, red-rimmed eyes, hands that twist constantly at a black ribbon.
cast.dress: Deep mourning black, unrelieved but for a thin strand of jet beads.
cast.voice_note: soft and halting, quick to apologise for her own tears

cast.name: Mrs Honoria Pike
cast.station: widow of a naval surgeon; three hundred a year and a house on the green
cast.want: to be first with the news, and proven right about it
cast.appearance: Short and broad, with grey hair pinned severely under a lace cap, and small quick eyes set in a round weathered face.
cast.dress: Black bombazine with a plain white fichu, ten years out of fashion and immaculately kept.
cast.voice_note: warm, talks too much, never doubts herself

cast.name: Mrs Hale
cast.station: draper's wife; keeps the counter of the circulating library above the shop
cast.want: to pass on exactly what she has heard, to everyone, the moment she has heard it
cast.appearance: Round-faced and pink, with spectacles pushed up into hair the colour of weak tea.
cast.dress: A striped apron over her gown, never removed even to serve customers upstairs.
cast.voice_note: reports gossip as news and news as gossip, precise and without malice

cast.name: Mr Silas Rowe
cast.station: curate of Amberlight; eighty a year and no expectations. Oversees the parish schoolroom fitted into the east wing of Amberlight House since the summer of 1817
cast.want: to keep his schoolroom warm and his scholars out of the shut rooms next door
cast.appearance: Tall and thin, dark hair worn slightly too long, with the stoop of a man used to low doorways and a face that gives away more than he intends.
cast.dress: Worn black coat, carefully brushed, and linen that has been turned at the cuffs.

chapters.title: Lights Above the Schoolroom
beats: Dismissing his scholars from the east-wing schoolroom one dusk in late October, Mr Rowe sees candlelight moving behind the shuttered main windows of Amberlight House, dark these six years, and mentions it next morning at the draper's counter.

Mrs Hale reports a Mr Edward Harker has taken the main block by the Marchmont family's leave, as trustee for a young ward's bequest from the late Sir Edward Marchmont's estate, the family itself still never having come into the parish.
Through the same counter Phoebe Langton is handed a curt note, signed only with initials, ordering full mourning made up within the week for a 'Miss Fairfax.'
Mrs Pike declares that a house does not light itself after six years dark unless something is being kept from the parish, and tells Phoebe to look sharp about her when she carries the order up.

chapters.title: The Measuring
beats: Harker receives Phoebe in the cold front hall, will not let her see Miss Fairfax, and hands her an old gown to take the measurements from instead.
Phoebe tells him plainly that a tradeswoman is owed the same civility as any customer, and he answers that her business is the cloth, not his household's affairs.
Through a part-opened door Phoebe glimpses Augusta Fairfax in unrelieved black, quietly weeping over a packet of letters, plainly grieved and not raving.
Harker abruptly cancels the order, presses payment well above its worth into Phoebe's hand, and shows her out, leaving her certain she has been paid to keep silent.

chapters.title: An Account Settled
beats: By Saturday Mrs Pike has the story whole, with a chained door added, and Mrs Hale repeats word for word what two scholars claim to have heard crying through the schoolroom wall.
Phoebe calls at the draper's to settle her own running account for thread and trim, and finds it already paid in full; Mrs Hale says a gentleman's man came in, paid in coin, and gave no name.
Phoebe recognises the hand on the receipt as the same curt hand that wrote Harker's cancelled order, and sets out up the lane meaning to return the money to his face.
She finds the front door of Amberlight House standing open, and hears from above a fall and a man's voice calling a name in open fear.

chapters.title: What the House Hid
beats: Phoebe runs up and finds Augusta fainted beside an overturned trunk of letters, with Harker kneeling over her and every coldness gone out of him.

Revived, Augusta tells Phoebe that her engagement was broken that spring when her intended's family called her a fortune-hunter over the Marchmont bequest, so she came away where no one knew her face.

Harker admits he settled Phoebe's account himself, ashamed of having wronged her over the cancelled order, and kept his name off it, since any known kindness from the house would set the parish asking why it burned lamps at all.
Voices carry up from below: Mrs Pike and Mrs Hale have followed the lit windows to the open front door.

chapters.title: Every Window Lit
beats: Phoebe and Harker meet the two women in the hall and give them the plain truth of a broken engagement and a cruel family, which ends the madwoman story outright.
Mrs Pike at once declares she always suspected grief rather than madness, and turns to prophesying an understanding between Phoebe and Harker, which Mrs Hale promises to repeat exactly as heard.
On Monday, Augusta, dressed at last in mourning Phoebe has properly made for her, crosses to the east wing with Mr Rowe and offers to hear the youngest scholars read.
At dusk Phoebe and Harker walk down the lane and exchange the apology neither gave before, while behind them every window of Amberlight House stands lit, the schoolroom's included.

Move the story to late autumn 1818 so it agrees with the series bible: Amberlight House stood empty from spring 1812 until summer 1817, and since summer 1817 its old east wing has been the parish schoolroom, fitted at the estate's charge. The rest of the house stayed shut until now.

Change these:
- Setting: "Amberlight parish, Hampshire, late autumn 1818".
- Logline: keep its shape and its turn, but the house has been shut six years, not ten, and only its main rooms light again — the east wing has been a schoolroom for a year.
- Cast: keep Miss Eliza Combe as protagonist, unchanged. Keep the trustee as love interest but give him a new first name (Nathaniel is already used in this parish). Keep the grieving young cousin, but she must not carry the Marchmont surname; give her a new surname, and make her a ward whose bequest came from the late Sir Edward Marchmont's estate. The trustee holds the main block of the house for her by leave of the Marchmont family, who still have not moved in themselves. Ages of recurring characters move forward one year from the bible's 1817 ages.
- Mr Silas Rowe is married by 1818; his wife is Mrs Rowe (formerly Miss Judith Vane). If she appears, copy her bible entry and call her Mrs Rowe. Do not give Mr Rowe arrears "from the Marchmont living" — a curate is paid by the rector, not the patron. Drop the arrears entirely.
- Put Mrs Hale, the draper's wife who keeps the library counter, into the cast as the channel the gossip runs through, alongside Mrs Pike. Eliza's dressmaking takes work through the draper's rather than competing with it.

Replace these wholesale: the chapters and their beats. Five chapters, 3 to 4 concrete beats each — things that happen, not moods.

Story requirements for the new chapters:
- Use the schoolroom as the gothic contrast: children's voices in the lit east wing by day, the shuttered main rooms by night. Mr Rowe teaches or oversees the school there, which is how the parish first learns the main rooms are occupied.
- The trustee's secret kindness stays the heart of it, but the parish must NOT credit Mrs Pike with an anonymous payment, and there is no anonymous payment to Mr Rowe. Mrs Pike's wrong guess is the madwoman. Eliza is the one who traces the kindness back to the trustee herself, through her own settled account.
- No disputed will plot and no apothecary's records as evidence. The cousin's grief and a broken engagement remain the hidden truth.
- Nothing may depend on having seen another Amberlight story.
